Clinical Molecular Genetics

Updated Oct 8, 2026 Revision 1.0 6 learning objectives

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Use restriction enzyme digestion to find a known point mutation (achondroplasia).
  2. LO 2Explain how an allele-specific ligation assay detects CF variants, and why a negative carrier screen still leaves risk.
  3. LO 3Detect large deletions and duplications with multiplex PCR and MLPA (Duchenne/Becker).
  4. LO 4Size repeat expansions with triplet-primed PCR (fragile X).
  5. LO 5Explain imprinting and use methylation analysis to diagnose Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.
  6. LO 6Choose and interpret Sanger, exome and genome sequencing, including variant classes, incidental findings and ethics.

MAPMatch the mutation type to the test

LO 1Restriction digest: achondroplasia

Q1. What causes achondroplasia?
  • Most common short-limbed dwarfism; autosomal dominant; ≈80% de novo
  • Gene FGFR3: normally limits bone growth → pathogenic variants make it constitutively active (gain of function)
  • Most have p.Gly380Arg: 99% a G→A transition (purine for purine), 1% a G→C transversion
  • De novo mutations arise exclusively on the paternal allele
Step 1

Rhizomelic (proximal) limb shortening, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, normal intelligence; associated with advanced paternal age.

Memory tool

FGFR3 is a brake; achondroplasia jams the brake on. Transition = same ring type (A↔G, C↔T); transversion = purine ↔ pyrimidine.

Q2. How does the restriction digest test work?
  1. PCR-amplify a 164 bp piece of exon 10
  2. Digest: SfcI cuts c.1138G>A → 109 + 55 bp; MspI cuts c.1138G>C → 107 + 57 bp
  3. Run on a gel: the variant creates the cut site, so mutant alleles give the smaller bands
GenotypeBands after SfcI
Wild type (aa)164 bp only (uncut)
Heterozygous (Aa)164 + 109 + 55 bp
Homozygous (AA)109 + 55 bp

Restriction digest gel

  • Lane C (het control): 164 + 109 + 55; patients D–F uncut = negative
Trap

Read the gel the right way round: here the mutation creates the restriction site. Extra (smaller) bands = variant present; one uncut band = normal.

Q3. When is testing used, and what if both parents are affected?
  • Confirm a clinical diagnosis; prenatal diagnosis when short limbs are seen on ultrasound; prenatal diagnosis when both parents have achondroplasia
  • Aa × Aa → 25% AA (homozygous: lethal), 50% Aa (achondroplasia), 25% aa (average stature)
  • Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is intermediate between the two homozygotes → you can read genotype from phenotype

Incomplete dominance

  • RR red · Rr pink · rr white

ApplyLO 1 application question

A1Two parents with achondroplasia ask about each pregnancy. Risks?
25% homozygous (lethal), 50% achondroplasia, 25% average stature.

LO 2Oligonucleotide ligation assay: cystic fibrosis

Q1. What should I know about CFTR?
  • Most common fatal AR disease in Caucasians; CFTR at 7q31; 27 exons; >2,000 pathogenic variants
  • ΔF508 most common; p.W1282* on 60% of Ashkenazi CF chromosomes; c.3120+1G>A common in African Americans (12.3%)
GroupCarrier frequency
Caucasian / Ashkenazi Jewish1 in 25
Hispanic1 in 45
African American1 in 62
Asian1 in 150

CF diagnosis: one of…

  • Characteristic clinical feature
  • Family history
  • Positive newborn screen

AND one of…

  • Positive sweat chloride ×2
  • Two CFTR mutations
  • Positive nasal transmembrane potential
Q2. How does the OLA work?
  1. PCR-amplify the CFTR region; denature to single strands
  2. Add a wild-type probe and a mutant probe (different labels) plus a common probe that sits right next to them
  3. DNA ligase joins probes only when the base at the junction is a perfect match
  4. Separate the ligated products by electrophoresis
Peaks seenGenotype
Wild-type onlyNon-carrier
Wild-type + mutantCarrier
Mutant onlyAffected (homozygous)

OLA principle

  • Ligase seals only a perfect match

Homozygous ΔF508

  • Mutant peak only at F508
Analogy — the zipper

Ligase is a zipper that only closes if the last tooth fits. Each probe tests one tooth: wild type or mutant.

Q3. Why test CF DNA, and what does a negative screen mean?
  • Genotype–phenotype; therapy depends on the variant
  • Diagnosis when sweat chloride is equivocal or the baby is too young
  • Prenatal diagnosis; routine prenatal/Ashkenazi carrier screening; male infertility work-up (CBAVD)
  • A negative carrier screen ≠ not a carrier: panels miss rare variants → calculate residual risk with Bayes
High yield

Residual risk example: prior carrier risk 1/25, panel detects 90%. Residual = (1/25 × 0.10) ÷ (1 − 1/25 × 0.90) ≈ 1/241.

Step 1

CFTR modulators (ivacaftor, elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) work only for specific variant classes; ΔF508 is a misfolding (trafficking) defect.

LO 3Multiplex PCR and MLPA: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

Q1. What kinds of DMD mutations exist?
  • X-linked; dystrophin is huge (2.4 Mb, 79 exons)
  • Large deletions ≈60% (98% detectable by multiplex PCR) · premature stops ≈15% · duplications ≈5%
  • Deletion size doesn't predict phenotype; the reading frame does: in-frame → truncated but partly functional protein (amino + carboxy ends kept) → Becker (milder, allelic)

Dystrophin deletions

  • A 46% in-frame deletion → mild Becker
Memory tool

"Frame, not size": out-of-frame → Duchenne (Destroyed protein); in-frame → Becker (Better).

Q2. How does MLPA find deletions and duplications?
  • Like OLA: paired probes hybridize side-by-side and are ligated, then all are amplified with one primer pair
  • Each probe pair has a unique length → separated by electrophoresis
  • Peak height = relative copy number vs a reference: shorter peak = deletion; taller = duplication

MLPA

  • Quantitative: dosage of each exon
Trap — gonadal mosaicism

A mother of an affected son can test negative in blood yet have a second affected son: the mutation is in her germline. Never quote zero recurrence.

Q3. Why does knowing the mutation matter?
  • Guides therapy: exon skipping (eteplirsen) restores the reading frame; ribosomal read-through (ataluren) for premature stops
  • Females may have a classic dystrophinopathy or be asymptomatic carriers
  • Males with DMD don't reproduce; males with BMD can
Step 1

DMD: Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, ↑↑ CK, dilated cardiomyopathy. Frameshift → DMD; in-frame → BMD.

LO 4Triplet-primed PCR: fragile X

Q1. How does a CGG expansion cause fragile X?
  • Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability in males
  • CGG repeat in the 5′ UTR of FMR1 expands to >200 → promoter methylation → gene silenced → loss of function
  • Repeats are dynamic: they expand as they pass through generations (tri-, tetra-, pentanucleotide repeats)
RepeatsCategoryMeaning
6–44NormalNo risk (most ≈29–30)
45–54Intermediate (gray)In general population; precursor in FXS grandparents
55–200PremutationMild learning issues; females can have affected children; early menopause (20% <40 y); older males (some females) → neuropathy/FXTAS
>200Full mutationAll males affected; ≈⅓ of females

One gene, three disorders

  • Premutation → FXTAS, POI; full → fragile X
High yield

Expansion happens when passed by the mother. 56 is the smallest repeat seen to expand to a full mutation in one generation.

Trap — never say never

Rare deletions or inactivating point mutations in FMR1 cause fragile X with a normal repeat count.

Step 1

Long face, large ears, prominent jaw, macroorchidism, joint laxity, MVP, autism. Classic old test: Southern blot.

Q2. How does triplet-primed PCR size the repeat?
  • Three primers: a labeled forward primer 5′ of the repeat, a reverse primer 3′ of it, and a second reverse primer that binds within the CGG repeat at many sites
  • Products form a "ladder" of peaks; run on a capillary sequencer → count repeats; a ladder that runs off the scale = full mutation

TP-PCR primers

  • One primer lands inside the repeat

Results

  • (a) male 32 · (b) female 20/64 premutation · (c) female 29/>200 full

ApplyLO 4 application question

A1A man with 100 CGG repeats asks about his children. Risks?
Expansion to full mutation occurs through mothers: all his daughters inherit a premutation (unaffected but at risk for POI and affected children); sons get his Y, so they're unaffected.

LO 5Imprinting: Prader-Willi and Angelman

Q1. How do PWS and Angelman differ clinically?

Prader-Willi

  • Severe hypotonia and feeding difficulty in infancy
  • Then hyperphagia → morbid obesity
  • Delayed milestones, cognitive impairment, hypogonadism
  • 1/10,000–1/20,000

Angelman

  • Severe developmental delay, ID, speech impairment
  • Gait ataxia; inappropriately happy demeanor with laughing
  • Microcephaly, seizures
  • 1/20,000
Memory tool

PWS = Paternal copy missing. Angelman = mAternal copy missing ("Maternal → Angelman, Happy puppet").

Q2. What is imprinting?
  • Different modification and expression of alleles depending on the parent of origin
  • The imprinted allele = the silent, inactivated one
  • Paternally imprinted gene → expressed from the maternal allele: UBE3A (Angelman)
  • Maternally imprinted genes → expressed from the paternal allele: SNRPN, ZNF127 (PWS)
  • During gametogenesis imprints are erased and reset by the individual's own sex → you re-imprint the chromosome from your opposite-sex parent

Imprint reset

  • Each generation reprograms by sex
Trap — terminology

"Maternally imprinted" = mom's copy is silenced, so the paternal copy is the working one. Lose dad's working copy at 15q11–q13 → PWS.

Q3. What mechanisms cause PWS and AS?
MechanismPWSAS
Deletion 15q11–q1370% (paternal)68% (maternal)
Uniparental disomy25% (maternal UPD)7% (paternal UPD)
Imprinting defect<5%3%
Translocation<1%<1%
Single gene—11% (UBE3A)
Other—10% (normal tests)
Step 1

Maternal UPD often arises from trisomy rescue (a trisomic zygote loses the paternal copy). UPD also matters for recessive disease: both copies from one carrier parent.

Q4. How does methylation-specific PCR make the diagnosis?
  • >96% of Cs in the PWS/AS critical region are methylated on the maternal allele; none on the paternal
  • Bisulfite converts unmethylated C → U; methylated C is protected
  • Primers specific for C (maternal, 174 bp) or U (paternal, 100 bp) + a common primer
  • Only maternal band → PWS; only paternal band → AS
  • Detects deletions, UPD and imprinting defects (≈99% of PWS, ≈78% of AS); misses UBE3A mutations

Methylation PCR gel

  • NL: both · AS: paternal only · PW: maternal only
High yield — why the mechanism matters
  • Deletion, UPD: recurrence <1/1,000
  • Imprinting center mutation: up to 50% (if inherited)
  • Chromosomal rearrangement: up to 50%; disorder depends on the transmitting parent's sex
  • UBE3A mutation: up to 50% if mother carries it
  • PWS and AS in cousins → think a familial translocation involving 15q11–q13

LO 6Sanger, exome and genome sequencing

Q1. How does Sanger sequencing work, and what does it miss?
  • Dideoxynucleotides (no 3′-OH) stop chain extension; color-labeled ends are read in order (T red, A green, C blue, G black)
  • Detects point mutations (missense, nonsense, synonymous, splice), small indels (frameshifts), mosaicism

Strengths

  • "Gold standard"
  • Accurate base-by-base read

Limitations

  • One sample/amplicon at a time
  • Can't detect large deletions/duplications
  • Poor for large repeat expansions
  • Allelic dropout (SNP under the primer)
  • May miss low-level mosaicism

Heterozygous variant

  • Double peak at the variant base

Mosaicism

  • Small second peak (arrow)
Trap — allelic dropout

A SNP under a primer stops one allele from amplifying → a heterozygote looks homozygous, and a pathogenic variant on that allele is missed.

Q2. How are variants classified?

ACMG/AMP five tiers: Pathogenic · Likely pathogenic · Variant of uncertain significance (VUS) · Likely benign · Benign.

  • VUS: find others with the same phenotype (e.g., GeneMatcher) or do functional lab work
Trap

A VUS is not actionable: don't change management or test relatives on a VUS alone.

Q3. Exome vs genome: what does each cover?
Exome (ES)Genome (GS)
Covers1–2% of the genome (≈80% of known exons); 85% of known Mendelian variants are in exons or splice sitesNearly everything
Variants found15,000–20,000≈3 million; ≈165 homozygous loss-of-function
MissesUnknown genes/exons, non-coding regulatory elements, introns, non-canonical splice sitesHigh-GC regions, large repeats, centromeres, telomeres
Diagnostic yield3–70% depending on indication (neurologic 22–68%)
  • Phenotypes caused by many genes → multigene panels (can cost ≈$6,000) or ES/GS
  • No answer? Heterogeneity, mutation in an un-analyzed region, or too many candidate variants (homozygosity)
  • CF by exome still must test the 23-variant ACMG panel: 2 deep intronic variants are invisible to exomes
  • ≈4–5% of patients with a clinical exome have two single-gene disorders (more with consanguinity or UPD)
Q4. What are incidental (secondary) findings and the ethical issues?
  • Incidental findings: results unrelated to the reason for testing. ACMG keeps a list of highly penetrant, medically actionable genes to return regardless of indication (ACMG-59 in 2016 → SF v3.0 with 73 genes, updated yearly)
  • Pre-test counseling: VUS, misattributed paternity, false positives/negatives, carrier status, late-onset disease, susceptibility alleles
  • Minors: normally not tested for adult-onset disorders (choose at 18), but ACMG recommends returning some such results found in a minor because of benefit to the family
High yield

Exome done for developmental delay incidentally shows a pathogenic BRCA1 variant → return it (penetrant, actionable), as covered in pre-test counseling.

Q5. What are the problems with direct-to-consumer testing?
  • Mostly SNP-based; companies interpret risk differently; patients bring reports to their physician
  • "Talent" tests make unsupported claims
  • Ancestry ("recreational genetics"): can strip ethnic identity, reveal misattributed paternity and family secrets, and feed forensic databases
  • Health tests: e.g., BRCA1/2 for only 3 Ashkenazi founder variants (not the most common in the general population); ≈40% of variants in DTC raw data are false positives
Trap

A negative DTC BRCA result does not rule out hereditary breast/ovarian cancer; confirm any positive in a clinical lab.

ApplyLO 6 application questions

A1A child has a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental phenotype and normal microarray. Best next test?
Exome (or genome) sequencing with pre-test counseling.
A2Which test detects a whole-exon deletion that Sanger missed?
MLPA (or microarray/multiplex PCR): Sanger can't see large deletions.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1FGFR3 testing: a 164 bp PCR product is digested with SfcI. The patient shows 164, 109 and 55 bp bands. Interpretation?

The variant creates the SfcI site: one cut + one uncut allele.

2Achondroplasia de novo mutations arise:

Exclusively paternal (advanced paternal age).

3In an oligonucleotide ligation assay, a patient shows only the mutant-probe peak at F508. Genotype?

Mutant only → homozygous mutant.

4A Caucasian woman tests negative on a CF carrier panel that detects 90% of mutations. What is true?

Negative screen ≠ non-carrier; residual risk ≈1/241.

5A boy with a large in-frame dystrophin deletion is likely to have:

Reading frame, not size: in-frame → partly functional protein → BMD.

6Which method gives relative copy number for each exon of a gene?

MLPA = dosage (deletions/duplications).

7A mother of a son with DMD has a negative blood test for his deletion. She then has a second affected son. Explanation?

Mutation confined to her germline.

8A woman has 80 CGG repeats in FMR1. Which is she most at risk of?

Premutation (55–200): POI and maternal expansion to full mutation.

9Methylation-specific PCR of 15q11–q13 shows only the maternal (methylated) band. Diagnosis?

No paternal contribution → PWS.

10Which Angelman mechanism carries a recurrence risk up to 50% if the mother also carries it?

Deletions and UPD recur <1/1,000; UBE3A or imprinting-center mutations up to 50%.

11Which limitation of Sanger sequencing explains a missed whole-exon deletion?

The remaining allele amplifies normally, hiding a heterozygous deletion.

12An exome for developmental delay incidentally finds a pathogenic BRCA1 variant. Per ACMG, this should be:

ACMG secondary-findings genes are penetrant and actionable.
